910.name: Early Slavic Settlements & Baltic Tribes
910.description: The territory of modern Belarus was inhabited by Baltic tribes before Slavic migrations in the 6th–7th centuries CE. Dregovichi, Radimichi, and Krivichi tribal unions settled the marshlands and river basins, establishing agrarian communities.

sub_clusters.name: Baltic Tribes & Pre-Slavic Era
sub_clusters.description: Baltic tribal groups inhabited the Pripyat marshes and Dnieper basin. Archaeological evidence from Milograd and Zarubintsy cultures reflects mixed Baltic-Slavic settlement patterns.

sub_clusters.name: Slavic Migration & Tribal Unions
sub_clusters.description: The Dregovichi, Krivichi, and Radimichi tribal unions settled the river systems of the Dnieper, Dvina, and Pripyat, establishing fortified settlements (gorodishcha) and agrarian communities.

920.name: Polotsk Principality & Early Statehood
920.description: The Principality of Polotsk emerged as the first significant political entity on Belarusian territory, rivalling Kyiv and Novgorod. Christianisation, dynastic rivalries, and trade along the Dvina-Dnieper corridor defined this era.

sub_clusters.name: Rise of Polotsk Principality
sub_clusters.description: Polotsk emerged as a powerful principality under Rogvolod and later Vseslav the Sorcerer (r. 1044–1101), competing with Kyiv for regional dominance. The Saint Sophia Cathedral in Polotsk was built in the mid-11th century.
key_events: Reign of Vseslav the Sorcerer of Polotsk (1044–1101)

sub_clusters.name: Fragmentation & Mongol-Era Pressures
sub_clusters.description: The Polotsk lands fragmented into appanage principalities. Crusader pressure from the Livonian Order on the Dvina frontier and Mongol incursions to the south reshaped regional power balances.

920.name: Grand Duchy of Lithuania & Belarusian Lands
920.description: Belarusian territories became the demographic and cultural core of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania (GDL). Old Belarusian (Ruthenian) served as the official state language, and the region's cities flourished under Magdeburg Law.

sub_clusters.name: GDL Expansion & Ruthenian Culture
sub_clusters.description: Lithuanian grand dukes Mindaugas, Gediminas, and Algirdas incorporated Belarusian principalities. Old Belarusian became the administrative language, and Orthodox Christianity remained dominant.

sub_clusters.name: Union with Poland & Magdeburg Law
sub_clusters.description: The Union of Krewo (1385) and subsequent dynastic ties with Poland. Belarusian cities received Magdeburg rights, and the Statute of Lithuania codified law in Old Belarusian.
key_events: Union of Krewo (1385) linking Lithuania and Poland

930.name: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth Era
930.description: The Union of Lublin (1569) merged the Grand Duchy of Lithuania with Poland. Belarusian lands experienced Polonisation and Catholicisation, the Uniate Church of Brest (1596), devastating Russo-Polish wars, and the Swedish Deluge.

sub_clusters.name: Union of Lublin & Polonisation
sub_clusters.description: The Union of Lublin (1569) created the Commonwealth. Belarusian nobility gradually adopted Polish language and culture, while Francysk Skaryna printed the first Belarusian-language Bible in 1517.

sub_clusters.name: Union of Brest & 17th-Century Wars
sub_clusters.description: The Union of Brest (1596) created the Greek Catholic (Uniate) Church, dividing Belarusian society. The devastating Russo-Polish War (1654–1667) and the Swedish Deluge killed up to half the population.

940.name: Russian Empire: Partitions & Imperial Rule
940.description: Belarus was absorbed into the Russian Empire through the three partitions of Poland (1772, 1793, 1795). Russification policies suppressed Belarusian identity, while the Pale of Settlement concentrated Jewish life in Belarusian cities.

sub_clusters.name: Partitions & Incorporation into Russia
sub_clusters.description: The three partitions of Poland-Lithuania (1772, 1793, 1795) placed all Belarusian lands under Russian control. The 1830 November Uprising led to further repressive measures.
key_events: First Partition of Poland (1772) — eastern Belarus to Russia

sub_clusters.name: Russification & the Jewish Pale of Settlement
sub_clusters.description: Tsarist Russification banned Belarusian-language printing and dissolved the Uniate Church (1839). The Pale of Settlement made Belarusian cities major centres of Jewish life, culture, and the emerging Zionist movement.

sub_clusters.name: Belarusian National Awakening
sub_clusters.description: The 1905 Revolution enabled Belarusian cultural societies and the newspaper Nasha Niva. An emerging intelligentsia articulated Belarusian national identity distinct from Polish and Russian frameworks.

950.name: World Wars & Byelorussian SSR
950.description: Belarus suffered catastrophically in both world wars. The brief Belarusian People's Republic (1918) was followed by Soviet annexation. WWII devastated Belarus: Nazi occupation killed approximately one in four Belarusians, destroyed 209 cities, and obliterated the Jewish population.

sub_clusters.name: Revolution, BPR & Soviet Annexation
sub_clusters.description: The short-lived Belarusian People's Republic (March 1918) was overrun by the Bolsheviks. The Byelorussian SSR was established (1919), and the Treaty of Riga (1921) partitioned Belarus between Soviet Russia and Poland. Soviet Belarus experienced Belarusianisation in the 1920s followed by Stalinist purges.

sub_clusters.name: WWII: Nazi Occupation & Devastation
sub_clusters.description: The Soviet invasion of eastern Poland (1939) unified Belarusian lands. Nazi Germany's Operation Barbarossa (1941) brought three years of brutal occupation: 2.2 million killed (including virtually the entire Jewish population), 628 villages destroyed (including Khatyn), and a massive partisan resistance movement.
key_events: Khatyn massacre (March 22, 1943) — symbol of Nazi atrocities
Liberation of Minsk (July 3, 1944) during Operation Bagration

950.name: Soviet Reconstruction & Chernobyl
950.description: Post-war reconstruction transformed Belarus into a Soviet industrial showcase. The Chernobyl disaster (1986) contaminated approximately 23% of Belarusian territory, triggering a national awakening and anti-Soviet sentiment.

sub_clusters.name: Post-War Industrialisation & Russification
sub_clusters.description: Massive reconstruction rebuilt Minsk as a Soviet model city. Belarusian SSR became a major industrial centre (tractors, electronics, petrochemicals) while Russification suppressed Belarusian language and culture.

sub_clusters.name: Chernobyl Fallout & National Revival
sub_clusters.description: The Chernobyl disaster (April 26, 1986) contaminated vast areas of southern Belarus. The Kurapaty mass grave discovery (1988) exposed Stalinist repressions, fuelling the Belarusian Popular Front movement and sovereignty declaration (1990).

960.name: Independence & Lukashenko's Authoritarian Rule
960.description: Belarus declared independence in 1991 but under Lukashenko (president since 1994) reverted to authoritarian governance, close alignment with Russia, suppression of democratic opposition, and the brutal crackdown on mass protests in 2020.

sub_clusters.name: Early Independence & Lukashenko's Rise
sub_clusters.description: Brief democratic period under Shushkevich (1991–1994) ended with Lukashenko's election in 1994. Controversial referendums (1995, 1996, 2004) concentrated power, reversed national symbols, and established Russian as co-official language.

sub_clusters.name: 2020 Protests & Deepening Russian Alliance
sub_clusters.description: The fraudulent 2020 presidential election triggered the largest protests in Belarusian history. Brutal repression, mass arrests, forced Ryanair diversion (2021), and the facilitation of Russia's Ukraine invasion from Belarusian territory further isolated the regime internationally.
key_events: 2020 mass protests against fraudulent presidential election
Belarus used as staging ground for Russia's Ukraine invasion (February 2022)
